paragraphs.text: The main policy story is a delay to the Medicaid work requirements. Several outlets, including the NYT, STAT and Fierce Healthcare, report that the administration will let states hold off on enforcement until July 1, 2027, instead of the planned January 1 start. CMS is framing it as an optional grace period during which states can fix their eligibility systems without terminating anyone for noncompliance. The requirements had been expected to cost millions of people their coverage, so the delay pushes back coverage losses that hospitals and Medicaid-heavy insurers had been modeling. Elsewhere in policy, CMS is extending its moratorium on new Medicare home health and hospice enrollment by six months over fraud concerns. STAT reports Democrats are coalescing around Medicare expansion proposals. Fierce Pharma says industry experts expect heavier scrutiny of the administration's most-favored-nation drug pricing deals now that Congress has changed hands.

paragraphs.text: Biotech capital markets had a decent Friday. Windward Bio, a Novo Holdings-backed company developing respiratory drugs licensed from China, began trading on Nasdaq after a $175 million IPO at $17 a share. Sanofi added another $50 million in a concurrent private placement, which brings the total to the $225 million reported by Fierce Biotech and MedCity. Fierce notes the lead asset is a potential rival to the blockbuster asthma drug Tezspire. It also says Rezera postponed its own listing, citing market conditions, so the window is open but selective. Dealroom reports that Langlai raised a Series B after its first drug won approval in China. BioPharma Dive says five neurology startups have raised roughly $450 million in recent weeks, a sign that venture money is returning to brain drugs.

paragraphs.text: Large-cap pharma news centered on portfolio building and cost cutting. Endpoints says argenx, six months into Karen Massey's tenure as CEO, has done two acquisitions worth about $3.4 billion combined in potential value as it tries to broaden beyond Vyvgart. Pfizer raised its 2026 revenue forecast by $1.5 billion, per a Motley Fool piece, though the headline gives no detail on the drivers. Bloomberg, via Fierce Pharma, reports that AstraZeneca cut about 600 US respiratory and immunology sales jobs as part of a $1.5 billion savings plan. AstraZeneca also took an Imfinzi-plus-Padcev combination to a positive result in cisplatin-ineligible bladder cancer, a direct challenge to Keytruda, and withdrew an EU filing for an amyloidosis antibody that had failed two late-stage trials. Novo has filed its sickle cell drug, acquired in a roughly billion-dollar deal. Moderna says it is ready to manufacture its Merck-partnered cancer vaccine ahead of an FDA filing by year-end. Teva held its first R&D day, and Fierce says one analyst team called its peak-sales estimates possibly aspirational.

paragraphs.text: Smaller companies show the usual split between good news and restructuring. Rezolute's ersodetug hit its primary endpoint in a phase 3 trial in tumor hyperinsulinism, ahead of an FDA meeting on a separate indication. Cellectis will cut 70% of its workforce as it pivots to in vivo therapies. Milestone is cutting 20% of staff after Cardamyst sales reached just $1 million in the third quarter. Bristol Myers' research chief is leaving amid an R&D reorganization. Summit Therapeutics let go several launch team members, including its commercial chief, ahead of a high-stakes FDA decision. Gubra, the obesity partner of AbbVie and Boehringer, moved to co-CEOs after an abrupt CEO exit. Synchron paused trials of its second-generation brain implant and says the pause is not safety related.

paragraphs.text: On the provider and insurer side, CommonSpirit reported a $544 million operating loss to open fiscal 2027, blaming a weaker payer mix and rising costs despite solid volumes. Ardent Health is buying Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47 million, with a $200 million capital commitment over ten years and at least $30 million of annual EBITDA expected by year three. A Fierce report says health plans face a demanding 2027 as clients press them to prove value. WSJ's Heard on the Street argues that CVS spinning off its drugstores could leave shareholders better off even if it doesn't placate lawmakers. Separately, WSJ reports that measles elimination status for the US has reportedly been revoked by PAHO, per people familiar. WSJ also reports that the White House ordered the release of detained Chinese vapes after contact with allies of the president.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia is the market story. Huang resigned after revelations about extramarital affairs, and the stock has wiped out $573 billion of market value this week, MarketWatch says, for a sixth straight weekly decline. HSBC cut the stock to hold and said it will struggle until a new CEO is named, while Bloomberg calls it the ultimate key-man risk. The FT reports that Arm's Rene Haas was sounded out in the CEO search. Spillover to the wider market has been modest but real. The NYT said broader stocks held up, and WSJ headlines described US stocks as mixed and then lower as chip shares sold off. MarketWatch notes AMD and other chipmakers initially looked like beneficiaries but then slid as investors rethought the AI trade. Next week brings big tests for that trade, WSJ says. Alphaville flags that someone made around $200 million shorting Nvidia before the news. Treat the political angle as unsettled. The FT reports Trump will not raise the spy issue with Xi at next week's summit, while Bessent has blamed Commerce for not blacklisting Megaspeed.

paragraphs.text: Rates are the other pressure point. The FT says Treasuries had their worst week since last April's tariff shock after hot inflation data and hawkish Fed comments. Yields rose in both the US and Europe. The FT reports that Fed policymakers have floated a bigger rate rise in December, and WSJ says market pricing for another increase has strengthened after strong jobs and inflation prints. Goolsbee said the Fed has work to do on inflation, and Williams said inflation is still too high. Producer prices cooled in October but remain well above trend. In a structural move, WSJ reports that Chair Warsh is cutting the number of rate decisions, with no vote at next October's meeting. The WSJ Dollar Index rose 0.84% on the week to 98.34. Across the Atlantic, the Bank of England's Huw Pill said last week's quarter-point hike to 4% was significant but there is further to go. The FT also reports that German coalition disputes are holding up an ECB board appointment.

paragraphs.text: Energy markets are loosening even though the Iran war is not over. Bloomberg describes continued tanker attacks near Hormuz alongside ample crude supply. The FT says the IEA sees oil swinging to surplus as Gulf shipments rebound, though rebuilding depleted stockpiles will take months. Brent was roughly flat and WTI off 0.2% on Friday, both lower for a second week. MarketWatch cautions that a crude glut will not automatically lower diesel prices. Trump said earlier in the week that no Iran deal was needed, which complicates hopes for a settlement. Gold and silver posted weekly losses. WSJ warns that surging energy costs and supply-chain delays could drive another round of food inflation, with one source quoted as saying the worst is yet to come.

paragraphs.text: The credit angle on Nvidia is financing. CNBC says Huang's exit puts the company's AI financing approach in focus, with investors watching credit markets and neocloud exposure. The reporting gives no detail on specific exposures. Axios reports that Nscale, a neocloud, has ballooning debt and needs more as its IPO approaches. Taken together, these stories show how much of the AI buildout depends on leverage tied to a single chip supplier. A Seeking Alpha piece says AI jitters are creating both risks and opportunities in high yield. A separate Seeking Alpha note on the MUC muni fund flags its high yield and deep discount but also significant leverage risk. Both are opinion pieces rather than market data.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO dominates deal coverage, and it is moving fast. The FT says the planned listing is less than a week away and values the company at $1.5 trillion, while BigGo cites a valuation approaching $1.4 trillion. The NYT says banks are on a roadshow for what could be the largest public offering ever. The Times of India reports demand about six times supply, with the valuation under scrutiny. CEO Dario Amodei told the FT he is not super fussed about market turmoil. Crypto-linked outlets say Kraken is taking requests for an ANTx offer with a 5% spread, and CoinGape points to a November 19 date. MarketWatch warns bitcoin, now below $69,000, could fall further if investors sell crypto to fund Anthropic allocations. Short seller John Hempton calls AI compute fibre optics Mark II but says he would still buy. The FT adds that Sam Bankman-Fried would have made nearly $40 billion from his early stake. Motley Fool says Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft and Micron are buying, but the headline gives no detail. The NYT notes Nvidia held $48 billion in stakes in 229 private companies including Anthropic and OpenAI as of July, which links Huang's exit to the start-up world.
